description: In 1687, Newton published a simple and enormous idea: the same force makes an apple fall and keeps the Moon in its orbit. Here is what it changed.

hero.hook: An apple, the Moon, the planets: one single force explains them all.

blocks.text: Before Newton, a great deal was already known about the planets, thanks to **Galileo**, the Italian physicist of the 17th century, and **[[Johannes Kepler]]**, the astronomer who described elliptical orbits. What was missing was a clear link between what falls on Earth and what turns in the sky.

In **1687**, **Isaac Newton** published the *[[Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica]]*, the *Principia*, the founding work of classical physics. In it he argued that gravitation is **universal**: it acts everywhere, and always in the same way.

Kepler had described the paths of the planets with precise laws: orbits shaped like an **ellipse**, equal areas swept out in equal times. Galileo had studied falling bodies. But why do the planets stay on their tracks? What “pulls” them?

Newton's answer was a **gravitational attraction**, a force that draws two masses toward each other. The Earth pulls the Moon. The Sun pulls the Earth. And you pull a little on the Earth too, even if the effect is tiny.

blocks.caption: The apple story is mostly a legend, but the idea behind it is real

blocks.text: Two bodies attract each other with a force that grows with their **mass**, the amount of matter they contain, and weakens as they move apart. More precisely, the force falls off with the **square of the distance**. Double the distance and the pull drops to a quarter. The farther away you are, the faster it fades.

blocks.caption: The planets keep “falling” toward the Sun and keep missing it, and that is an orbit

blocks.text: The Moon is “falling” toward the Earth all the time. Because it also carries a large sideways speed, it circles around us instead of crashing into us.

Newton also set out three **laws of motion**. In short: an object keeps its speed when no force acts on it, the principle of **inertia**; a force changes that speed; every action meets an opposite reaction.
With those laws you can calculate trajectories, **tides**, the rise and fall of the oceans under the pull of the Moon and the Sun, and orbits. Physics became a tool for prediction.

Two centuries later, **[[Albert Einstein]]** corrected Newton for the extreme cases, very high speeds and very strong gravity, with [[Relativistic gravitation (Einstein)]]. Gravity became a curvature of space-time instead of an invisible force. But for launching a rocket or explaining the tides, Newton is still excellent.
Newton united the sky and the Earth: gravitation pulls on masses everywhere. It is one of the greatest syntheses in the history of science.

sections.title: Powerful, but not the last word
